If $\mathcal N_1,\mathcal N_2$ are such nets for the two unit spheres and $A$ is an $n\times N$ complex matrix, approximating unit vectors $u,v$ attaining $\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}=|u^*Av|$ gives
$$\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le (1-2\varepsilon)^{-1}\max_{u_0\in\mathcal N_1,\ v_0\in\mathcal N_2}|u_0^*Av_0|.$$
Indeed, the approximation error is at most $\|u-u_0\|\|A\|+\|v-v_0\|\|A\|\le2\varepsilon\|A\|$.

Fix deterministic unit vectors $u\in\mathbb C^n$ and $v\in\mathbb C^N$. Then $u^*X_nv=\sum_{i,j}\overline u_i v_j\xi_{ij}$ is a sum of independent centered complex variables. Independence, exponential Markov inequality [F3], and optimization in $\lambda$ therefore give
$$\mathbb P\{|u^*X_nv|>t\}\le4\exp\!\left(-\frac{t^2}{4K^2}\right),$$
because $\sum_{i,j}K^2|u_i|^2|v_j|^2=K^2$.

First fix a deterministic complex matrix $A$. Centering the diagonal terms gives
$$\xi^*A\xi-\operatorname{tr}A=\sum_iA_{ii}(|\xi_i|^2-1)+\sum_{i\ne j}\overline{\xi_i}A_{ij}\xi_j.$$
In the squared modulus, independence and $\mathbb E\xi_i=0$ make diagonal and off-diagonal parts uncorrelated; distinct diagonal terms are uncorrelated; and two off-diagonal terms have nonzero expectation only when their ordered index pairs agree or are reversed. Expanding those remaining terms yields
$$\mathbb E|\xi^*A\xi-\operatorname{tr}A|^2=(\mu_4-1)\sum_i|A_{ii}|^2+\sum_{i\ne j}|A_{ij}|^2+|\tau|^2\sum_{i\ne j}A_{ij}\overline{A_{ji}}.$$
Here $\mu_4-1\ge0$ by Cauchy–Schwarz, and $|\tau|\le\mathbb E|\xi_1|^2=1$. Also
$$\left|\sum_{i\ne j}A_{ij}\overline{A_{ji}}\right|\le\sum_{i\ne j}|A_{ij}||A_{ji}|\le\sum_{i\ne j}|A_{ij}|^2.$$
Thus the deterministic quadratic-form variance is at most $C_{\mu_4,\tau}\|A\|_F^2$.

By [F2], $(\xi,A)$ has product joint law. The integrand is integrable because
$$|\xi^*A\xi-\operatorname{tr}A|^2\le2\|A\|_F^2\|\xi\|_2^4+2d\|A\|_F^2,$$
and $\mathbb E\|\xi\|_2^4<\infty$ in finite dimension. Integrate the deterministic inequality from step 1.1 over the law of $A$; [F3] justifies the order of integration and gives the stated bound.

there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that

$$A:=\frac1N T^{1/2}XX^*T^{1/2}.$$
For each distinct eigenvalue $\lambda$ of the Hermitian matrix $A$, let $P_\lambda$ be the orthogonal projection onto its eigenspace. The empirical spectral distribution of $A$, normalized by its dimension $d$, is
$$\mu_A:=\frac1d\sum_{\lambda\in\operatorname{spec}(A)}\operatorname{rank}(P_\lambda)\,\delta_\lambda,$$
where $\delta_\lambda$ is the unit point mass at $\lambda$.
For a deterministic unit vector $x\in\mathbb C^d$, its directional spectral measure is
$$\mu_A^x:=\sum_{\lambda\in\operatorname{spec}(A)}\|P_\lambda x\|_2^2\,\delta_\lambda.$$
For a Borel set $B\subseteq\mathbb R$, set $\mathbf1_B(A):=\sum_{\lambda\in B\cap\operatorname{spec}(A)}P_\lambda$; then $\mu_A^x(B)=x^*\mathbf1_B(A)x$. Both measures are supported on the nonnegative real axis.

For every Hermitian positive semidefinite $A\in\mathbb C^{d\times d}$, its empirical spectral distribution $\mu_A$ is a Borel probability measure supported on $[0,\infty)$. For every deterministic unit vector $x\in\mathbb C^d$, its directional spectral measure $\mu_A^x$ is also a Borel probability measure supported on $[0,\infty)$.

Define
$$A_n=N_n^{-1}T_n^{1/2}X_nX_n^*T_n^{1/2},\qquad \widetilde A_n=N_n^{-1}X_n^*T_nX_n,$$
$$R_n(z)=(A_n-zI_n)^{-1},\qquad \widetilde R_n(z)=(\widetilde A_n-zI_{N_n})^{-1},\qquad q_n(z)=\mathbb E\left[N_n^{-1}\operatorname{tr}\widetilde R_n(z)\right].$$

$$s_1\ge\cdots\ge s_r>0,$$

$$Tv=\sum_{j=1}^r s_j\langle v,e_j\rangle f_j$$

for every $v\in V$.

Such f is Borel measurable (inverse images of open sets are open) and $\int|f|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\mu(S)<\infty$, so the integrals are finite in [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]. Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

For integer $K$, set $\xi^{(K)}=\xi\mathbf1_{\{|\xi|\le K\}}-\mathbb E[\xi\mathbf1_{\{|\xi|\le K\}}]$, $\sigma_K^2=\mathbb E|\xi^{(K)}|^2$, and $\Delta^{(K)}=\xi-\xi^{(K)}$. For all sufficiently large $K$, $\sigma_K>0$; put $\zeta^{(K)}=\xi^{(K)}/\sigma_K$. These entries are centered, bounded, iid and have unit second absolute moment, while $\Delta^{(K)}$ is centered iid with finite fourth moment. At matrix level, $X_n=\sigma_K Z_n^{(K)}+D_n^{(K)}$, where $Z_n^{(K)}$ and $D_n^{(K)}$ are the common upper-left blocks formed from $\zeta^{(K)}$ and $\Delta^{(K)}$.

$$\limsup_n\frac{\|X_n\|}{\sqrt{N_n}}\le C_c,\quad \limsup_n\frac{\|Z_n^{(K)}\|}{\sqrt{N_n}}\le C_c,\quad \limsup_n\frac{\|D_n^{(K)}\|}{\sqrt{N_n}}\le C_c\tau_K,$$

$$\limsup_n\|A_n-\sigma_K^2A_n^{(K)}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le M C_c^2(1+\sigma_K)\tau_K,

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, and let
$A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$. A matrix $B\in M_{n\times m}(\mathbb F)$ is a
**Moore--Penrose pseudoinverse** of $A$ when

$$ABA=A,\qquad BAB=B,$$

and the two square products are self-adjoint:

$$ (AB)^*=AB,\qquad (BA)^*=BA. $$

When such a matrix exists and is unique, it is denoted by $A^+$.

The four displayed relations are the **Penrose equations**. They are written in
the matrix product and adjoint conventions of
[[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]] and
[[thm-matrix-of-the-adjoint-is-the-conjugate-transpose]].

Let $M\in\mathbb F^{p\times q}$ be any finite real or complex matrix, and let $M^\dagger$ be its unique Moore-Penrose inverse. Then $P=MM^\dagger$ and $Q=M^\dagger M$ are self-adjoint idempotents. The range of $P$ is $\operatorname{Ran}(M)$, and the range of $Q$ is $\operatorname{Ran}(M^\dagger)$. Thus both are orthogonal projections. If $M$ has full row rank, then $MM^\dagger=I_p$.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces, and let $r$ be the number of positive singular values of $T$.
Then there exist orthonormal bases $(e_1,\dots,e_n)$ of $V$ and
$(f_1,\dots,f_m)$ of $W$, together with singular values

$$s_1\ge\cdots\ge s_r>0,$$

such that

$$Tv=\sum_{j=1}^r s_j\langle v,e_j\rangle f_j$$

for every $v\in V$.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. Then $\operatorname{rank} T$ equals the number of positive
singular values of $T$.

Let $(\xi_{ij})_{i,j\ge1}$ be one infinite iid array of real random variables with mean zero, variance one and finite fourth moment. For each $n$, let $X_n=(\xi_{ij})_{1\le i\le n,1\le j\le p_n}$ and suppose $p_n/n\to\gamma\in(0,\infty)$. Set $S_n=X_n^{\mathsf T}X_n/n$ and let $\lambda_{\min}^{+}(S_n)$ denote its smallest positive eigenvalue whenever one exists. If $\gamma<1$, then almost surely $X_n$ has full column rank for all sufficiently large $n$, so $S_n$ has no zero eigenvalues eventually and $\lambda_{\min}(S_n)\to(1-\sqrt\gamma)^2$. For each positive integer $n$, let $p_n$ be a positive integer with $p_n/n\to\gamma\in(0,\infty)$, and let $X_n\in\mathbb R^{n\times p_n}$ have mutually independent entries with one common law, mean zero, variance one, and finite fourth moment. Set $S_n=X_n^{\mathsf T}X_n/n$ and let $\mu_n$ be its empirical spectral distribution normalized by $p_n$. Then $\mu_n$ converges weakly almost surely to the probability measure with density
$$\rho_\gamma(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{\sqrt{(b_\gamma-x)(x-a_\gamma)}}{2\pi\gamma x},&a_\gamma<x<b_\gamma,\\0,&x\notin(a_\gamma,b_\gamma),\end{cases}\qquad a_\gamma=(1-\sqrt\gamma)^2,\quad b_\gamma=(1+\sqrt\gamma)^2,$$
and an atom of mass $(1-1/\gamma)_+$ at zero.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $(\xi_{ij})_{i,j\ge1}$ be one infinite iid array of complex random variables with $\mathbb E\xi_{11}=0$, $\mathbb E|\xi_{11}|^2=1$, and $\mathbb E|\xi_{11}|^4<\infty$. For each positive integer $n$, let $N_n$ be positive with $n/N_n\to c\in(0,\infty)$ and let $X_n=(\xi_{ij})_{1\le i\le n,\,1\le j\le N_n}$ be its upper-left block. Let $T_n$ be deterministic Hermitian positive semidefinite with uniformly bounded operator norm and empirical eigenvalue measures $H_n=n^{-1}\sum_i\delta_{\lambda_i(T_n)}\Rightarrow H$. Let $x_n\in\mathbb C^n$ be deterministic unit vectors such that, for every $w\in\mathbb C\setminus[0,\infty)$,
$$x_n^*(T_n-wI_n)^{-1}x_n\longrightarrow m_H(w):=\int_{[0,\infty)}(t-w)^{-1}\,dH(t).$$
Define $A_n=N_n^{-1}T_n^{1/2}X_nX_n^*T_n^{1/2}$ and $\mu_n^{x_n}(B)=x_n^*\mathbf1_B(A_n)x_n$ for Borel $B\subseteq[0,\infty)$. Then almost surely $\mu_n^{x_n}$ converges weakly to the probability measure $F_{c,H}$ whose Stieltjes transform is the unique $m\in\mathbb C$ satisfying $\operatorname{Im}m>0$, $u=-(1-c)/z+cm$ with $\operatorname{Im}u>0$, and
$$m=\int_{[0,\infty)}\frac{1}{t(1-c-czm)-z}\,dH(t),\qquad \operatorname{Im}z>0.$$

For $\gamma>0$, set
$$a_\gamma=(1-\sqrt\gamma)^2,\qquad b_\gamma=(1+\sqrt\gamma)^2,\qquad r_+:=\max\{r,0\}\quad(r\in\mathbb R).$$
Define the Marchenko–Pastur set function on Borel $A\subseteq\mathbb R$ by
$$\mu_\gamma(A):=\int_{A\cap(a_\gamma,b_\gamma)}\frac{\sqrt{(b_\gamma-x)(x-a_\gamma)}}{2\pi\gamma x}\,d\lambda(x)+\left(1-\frac1\gamma\right)_+\delta_0(A),$$
where $\lambda$ is Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R$. The formula defines a finite Borel measure; its total mass is established by the Marchenko–Pastur law below.

For every $\gamma>0$, the set function $\mu_\gamma$ in the definition of the Marchenko–Pastur measure is a Borel probability measure supported on $[0,\infty)$. For every $z\in\mathbb C$ with $\eta:=\operatorname{Im}z>0$, its Stieltjes transform $m_\gamma(z)$ satisfies
$$1+z m_\gamma(z)=\frac{m_\gamma(z)}{1+\gamma m_\gamma(z)},\qquad \operatorname{Im}\bigl(1-\gamma-z-\gamma z m_\gamma(z)\bigr)\le-\eta.$$

For Borel probability measures $\mu_n,\mu$ on a metric space S, write $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$ if $\int f\,d\mu_n\to\int f\,d\mu$ for every bounded continuous real function f on S. Continuity is [[def-metric-continuity]]. Such f is Borel measurable (inverse images of open sets are open) and $\int|f|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\mu(S)<\infty$, so the integrals are finite in [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]. No completeness or coupling is required.

Let $c>0$, let $H$ be a Borel probability measure on $[0,\infty)$, and fix $z\in\mathbb C$ with $\operatorname{Im}z>0$. There is at most one $q\in\mathbb C$ satisfying $\operatorname{Im}q>0$, $u:=-(1-c)/z+cq$ with $\operatorname{Im}u>0$, and
$$q=\int_{[0,\infty)}\frac{1}{t(1-c-czq)-z}\,dH(t).$$

For every $\gamma>0$, the set function $\mu_\gamma$ in the definition of the Marchenko–Pastur measure is a Borel probability measure supported on $[0,\infty)$. For every $z\in\mathbb C$ with $\eta:=\operatorname{Im}z>0$, its Stieltjes transform $m_\gamma(z)$ satisfies
$$1+z m_\gamma(z)=\frac{m_\gamma(z)}{1+\gamma m_\gamma(z)},\qquad \operatorname{Im}\bigl(1-\gamma-z-\gamma z m_\gamma(z)\bigr)\le-\eta.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

Put $P_{\ker X_n}=I_{p_n}-X_n^+X_n$. For any fixed $v\in\mathbb R^{p_n}$, $\mathbb E_{z_{0,n}}(z_{0,n}^{\mathsf T}v)^2=v^{\mathsf T}\mathbb E[z_{0,n}z_{0,n}^{\mathsf T}]v=\|v\|_2^2$, so the stated prediction risk equals $\mathbb E_{\varepsilon_n}[\|\widehat\beta_n-\beta_n\|_2^2\mid X_n]$. By [F2], $X_n^+X_n$ is the row-space projection, so $\widehat\beta_n-\beta_n=-P_{\ker X_n}\beta_n+X_n^+\varepsilon_n$. Conditional on $X_n$, the cross term has expectation zero because $\mathbb E[\varepsilon_n\mid X_n]=0$. Its noise contribution is
$$\mathbb E_{\varepsilon_n}\|X_n^+\varepsilon_n\|_2^2=\sigma^2\operatorname{tr}(X_n^+(X_n^+)^{\mathsf T})=\sigma^2\operatorname{tr}((X_n^{\mathsf T}X_n)^+)=\frac{\sigma^2}{n}\operatorname{tr}(S_n^+),$$
where the middle equality follows by writing an SVD and the last uses $(aB)^+=a^{-1}B^+$ for $a>0$. With $x_n=\beta_n/r$, this proves the exact identity
$$\mathcal R_n=r^2x_n^{\mathsf T}P_{\ker X_n}x_n+\frac{\sigma^2}{n}\operatorname{tr}(S_n^+).$$

Suppose $\gamma<1$ and set $a=(1-\sqrt\gamma)^2>0$. By [F4], $X_n$ has full column rank eventually and every eigenvalue of $S_n$ is at least $a/2$ eventually. Thus the bias term in step 1.1 is zero and $p_n^{-1}\operatorname{tr}(S_n^+)=\int f(t)d\mu_n(t)$ for the bounded continuous function $f(t)=1/\max(t,a/2)$. By [F5] and [F8], this converges to $J_\gamma=\int t^{-1}d\mu_\gamma(t)$, since the Marchenko–Pastur support is bounded below by $a$. For $s>0$, define $m_\gamma(-s)=\int(t+s)^{-1}d\mu_\gamma(t)$. The integrands are bounded by $1/a$ and converge pointwise to $1/t$, so [F10] gives $m_\gamma(-s)\to J_\gamma$ as $s\downarrow0$. The fixed-point equation in [F7], initially stated for $z\in\mathbb C^+$, extends to $z=-s<0$ by dominated convergence in its defining integral; its denominator stays nonzero because $1+\gamma m_\gamma(-s)>0$. Taking $s\downarrow0$ yields $1+(\gamma-1)J_\gamma=0$, hence $J_\gamma=1/(1-\gamma)$. Since $p_n/n\to\gamma$, step 1.1 gives $\mathcal R_n\to\sigma^2\gamma/(1-\gamma)$.

Suppose $\gamma>1$ and set $a=(\sqrt\gamma-1)^2>0$. By [F4], $X_n$ has full row rank eventually, $S_n$ has exactly $p_n-n$ zero eigenvalues, and all positive eigenvalues are at least $a/2$ eventually. The continuous function $g(t)=\max(1-2t/a,0)$ equals one at zero and vanishes on the positive spectrum for all sufficiently large $n$. Hence $x_n^{\mathsf T}P_{\ker X_n}x_n=\int g(t)d\mu_n^{x_n}(t)\to\int g(t)dF_{\gamma,\delta_1}(t)=1-1/\gamma$ by [F6], [F7], and [F9]; [F9] identifies the limit with $\mu_\gamma$, on whose positive support $g=0$ and whose zero atom has mass $1-1/\gamma$. Define $h(0)=0$ and, for $t>0$, $h(t)=t^{-1}\min(1,\max(0,4t/a-1))$. This is bounded and continuous, equals zero at zero, and equals $1/t$ for $t\ge a/2$. Therefore $p_n^{-1}\operatorname{tr}(S_n^+)=\int h(t)d\mu_n(t)\to J_\gamma^+:=\int_{(0,\infty)}t^{-1}d\mu_\gamma(t)$ by [F5] and [F8]. [F7] gives $m_\gamma(-s)=(1-1/\gamma)/s+J_\gamma^++o(1)$ as $s\downarrow0$: subtract the zero atom and use [F10] by dominated convergence on the positive support, whose lower endpoint is $a>0$. To compute the constant term, write $\alpha=1-1/\gamma$ and substitute $m=\alpha/s+J_\gamma^++o(1)$ into $1+(\gamma-1-s)m-\gamma s m^2=0$, the fixed-point equation at $z=-s$ (again obtained by dominated convergence from [F7]). The coefficient of $s^{-1}$ vanishes because $\gamma\alpha=\gamma-1$; the constant term is $1-\alpha-(\gamma-1)J_\gamma^++o(1)$. It must vanish, so $J_\gamma^+=1/[\gamma(\gamma-1)]$. Using $p_n/n\to\gamma$ in step 1.1 proves $\mathcal R_n\to r^2(1-1/\gamma)+\sigma^2/(\gamma-1)$.

all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.
